name: Attribution bias
statement: Attribution bias is a family label rather than one effect, and its members are measured apart, tested apart, and land anywhere from d = 0.095 to d = 1.82.
meaning: The label covers any claim that people assign causes in a slanted way. Its members share no measure and no common prediction. Malle separates two senses of the word attribution: explaining a behaviour, which answers a why question, and inferring a quality of the agent from the behaviour. Correspondence bias and hostile attribution belong to the second sense. The actor-observer hypothesis and the self-serving pattern belong to the first. What holds the family together is a scoring convention. An answer is coded as internal or external, and a bias is a departure from the split that some norm treats as correct. Members disagree about which way the departure runs. This page is a map of the members that have their own entries here, because that is the level at which the evidence exists.

origin.note: Malle calls Heider the undisputed founder of attribution work and argues that the person and situation dichotomy credited to him is not his. On Malle's reading Heider applied internal and external factors only to the 'can' forces that let an action outcome succeed, and explained intentional action by the actor's reasons instead. Malle quotes Kelley's 1967 paper for the general form, that in the attribution process 'the choice is between external attribution and internal … attribution', and calls that paper the first systematic treatment of lay causal explanation. Heider's book is cited here from its Crossref record and from Malle's account of it; Kelley's paper carries no DOI and is quoted at one remove through Malle. No single publication defines the umbrella term.

evidence: The family has been counted once at family level. Richard, Bond and Stokes-Zoota sorted 474 meta-analytic effects, resting on 33,912 primary estimates, into 18 topics, and report an overall mean of r = .21 with an across-literatures standard deviation of .15. Their attribution row holds 36 meta-analytic conclusions over 1,929 estimates at a mean of r = .14, with a mean corrected standard deviation of .14. Only social influence, at r = .13, is smaller. Inside their attribution appendix the two halves of the same claim come apart: people attributing successes to ability sits at r = .29 over 69 estimates and to internal factors at r = .26 over 49, while failures to bad luck sits at r = .10 over 69, failures to external factors at r = .09 over 42, and failures to task difficulty at r = .05 over 69. Those rows are Richard and colleagues summarising other people's meta-analyses, so they are quoted here at one remove and none is placed in a structured field. The method base is narrow across the family. Malle estimates that about 95% of all data on the fundamental attribution error come from tightly controlled laboratory experiments rather than surveys, observation or archives. Verhoef and colleagues report that almost 98% of their 219 hostile-attribution effect sizes came from studies using hypothetical stories.

replication.headline: No replication of attribution bias exists, because no experiment by that name exists. Five members have been tested and their results run from d = 0.095 to d = 1.82.
replication.detail: Correspondence bias held. Many Labs 2 re-ran Miyamoto and Kitayama's essay task and found writers assigned to argue for capital punishment rated at 10.98 against 4.45 for those assigned to argue against, d = 1.82 with a 95% confidence interval from 1.76 to 1.87 across 7,197 people; entry 11. The actor-observer asymmetry did not hold. Malle's abstract gives average effect sizes from d = -0.016 to d = 0.095 across 173 published studies and 14,686 participants; entry 152. The self-serving pattern held. Mezulis and colleagues put it at d = 0.96 across 266 studies, with Asian samples at 0.30 against 1.05 for United States samples, and Allen and colleagues found it outside the laboratory in 69 sport studies with 160 effect sizes and 10,515 athletes, at a standardised mean difference of 0.62 for personal outcomes and 0.63 for team outcomes; entry 109. Hostile attribution held at a modest size, d = 0.33, 95% confidence interval 0.28 to 0.39, across 111 studies and 29,272 participants; entry 140. The ultimate attribution error is unsettled: Hewstone's review of 19 studies finds an ingroup-favouring tendency in most of them and says the evidence gives only limited support to Pettigrew's error; entry 204. Those five verdicts are answers to five different questions. Averaging them would produce a number describing nothing.

limits: No meta-analysis, multi-site replication or registered report of attribution bias as a whole was located. Nor was any study that measured several members in the same sample and reported whether they cohere, which is what a reader would need before calling a person high or low in attribution bias generally. The search covered Crossref by bibliographic query for family-level meta-analyses and for intercorrelations among attribution measures, PubMed, and general web search. What it returned was work on single members and on attributional style questionnaires, which measure one member rather than the set. The Richard figures are a 2003 snapshot and average conclusions of unlike kinds, from laboratory success and failure tasks to depression research, so the r = .14 describes a literature rather than an effect. Membership of the family is a matter of convention. Hewstone alone splits intergroup attribution into three paradigms, and catalogues differ on which claims to admit, so the five mapped above are the members with entries on this site rather than an agreed list. Heider's 1958 book was read only through its Crossref record and Malle's account of it, and Kelley's 1967 paper only through Malle's quotation.
misreadings: The commonest error is treating one member's fate as the family's. Malle's meta-analysis is reported as the fall of the fundamental attribution error, and he writes the opposite in the same paper: one cannot conclude that because there is no actor-observer asymmetry in attributions, there is no fundamental attribution error. The reverse move is as common, with the correspondence bias result read as vindication of everything in the group. Summarising the family as a tendency to overweight disposition also fails, because members point in opposite directions. Pettigrew's second prediction is that a good act by an outgroup member draws a situational reading, and the self-serving pattern predicts external causes for a person's own failures. The internal and external columns are a coding scheme rather than categories the mind uses. Malle reports that codings of free verbal explanations into person and situation categories are oversensitive to linguistic surface patterns, and attributes part of the unexplained variance in his pool to the interpretational ambiguity of dichotomous person-situation scales. Whether a slanted attribution is an error is also open. Malle calls the question of what constitutes an error a thorny one and points to Funder and to Krueger and Funder for the argument. His broader question stands over the whole family: how a hypothesis could appear in textbooks for decades as supported by research while the cumulative evidence showed little support for it.
